def target_trial_emulation(df, id_col, treatment_col, outcome_col,
                           grace_period=30, max_followup=730):
    """
    Emulate a target trial with two strategies:
    - Strategy A: Initiate treatment within grace period and continue
    - Strategy B: Do not initiate treatment within grace period
    Uses cloning, censoring, and IPW to estimate per-protocol effects.
    """
    clone_treated = df.copy(); clone_treated['strategy'] = 1
    clone_control = df.copy(); clone_control['strategy'] = 0
    pooled = pd.concat([clone_treated, clone_control], ignore_index=True)
    pooled['clone_id'] = pooled.index

    # Censoring: deviate from assigned strategy
    treated_within_grace = pooled[treatment_col] == 1
    pooled['censored'] = False
    pooled.loc[(pooled['strategy'] == 1) & (~treated_within_grace), 'censored'] = True
    pooled.loc[(pooled['strategy'] == 0) & treated_within_grace, 'censored'] = True

    # Follow-up and outcome
    pooled['followup'] = max_followup
    pooled.loc[pooled['censored'], 'followup'] = grace_period
    pooled['event'] = pooled[outcome_col]
    pooled.loc[pooled['censored'], 'event'] = 0

    # IPW for censoring
    censor_covs = [c for c in df.columns if c not in [id_col, treatment_col, outcome_col, 'strategy']]
    y_unc = (~pooled['censored']).astype(int)
    X_c = pooled[censor_covs].fillna(0)
    if 0 < y_unc.sum() < len(y_unc):
        cm = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_c, y_unc)
        p_unc = cm.predict_proba(X_c)[:, 1].clip(0.01, 0.99)
        pooled['ipw_censor'] = np.where(pooled['censored'], 0, 1/p_unc)
    else:
        pooled['ipw_censor'] = 1.0

    uncensored = pooled[~pooled['censored']].copy()
    print(f"Cloned: {len(pooled)} (from {len(df)})")
    print(f"  Strategy A: {(pooled['strategy']==1).sum()} ({pooled[pooled['strategy']==1]['censored'].sum()} censored)")
    print(f"  Strategy B: {(pooled['strategy']==0).sum()} ({pooled[pooled['strategy']==0]['censored'].sum()} censored)")
    print(f"  Uncensored for analysis: {len(uncensored)}")
    return pooled

def ps_stratification(df, covariates, treatment_col='treatment',
                      ps_col='propensity_score', outcome_col=None,
                      n_strata=5, outcome_type='continuous'):
    """
    PS stratification (quintiles): estimate effect within strata and pool.
    """
    df = df.copy()
    df['ps_stratum'] = pd.qcut(df[ps_col], n_strata, labels=False)
    for s in range(n_strata):
        sd = df[df['ps_stratum'] == s]
        print(f"Stratum {s+1} (n={len(sd)}, PS [{sd[ps_col].min():.3f}, {sd[ps_col].max():.3f}]):")
        for cov in covariates[:5]:
            smd = compute_smd(sd, cov, treatment_col)
            print(f"  {cov}: SMD={abs(smd):.4f} {'OK' if abs(smd)<0.1 else 'IMBALANCED'}")
    if outcome_col:
        effects = []
        for s in range(n_strata):
            sd = df[df['ps_stratum'] == s]
            t, c = sd[sd[treatment_col]==1], sd[sd[treatment_col]==0]
            if outcome_type == 'continuous':
                eff = t[outcome_col].mean() - c[outcome_col].mean()
            else:
                eff = t[outcome_col].mean() - c[outcome_col].mean()
            w = len(sd) / len(df)
            effects.append((s, eff, w))
        pooled = sum(e * w for _, e, w in effects)
        print(f"\nPooled effect (stratified): {pooled:.4f}")
        for s, e, w in effects:
            print(f"  Stratum {s+1}: effect={e:.4f}, weight={w:.3f}")
        return pooled

def baseline_table(data, covariates, treatment_col='treatment',
                   categorical_cols=None, weight_col=None):
    """Produce Table 1: baseline characteristics by treatment group."""
    categorical_cols = categorical_cols or []
    rows = []
    for cov in covariates:
        t, c = data[data[treatment_col]==1], data[data[treatment_col]==0]
        if weight_col:
            wt, wc = t[weight_col].values, c[weight_col].values
            if cov in categorical_cols:
                mt = f"{np.average(t[cov], weights=wt)*100:.1f}%"
                mc = f"{np.average(c[cov], weights=wc)*100:.1f}%"
            else:
                mt = f"{np.average(t[cov], weights=wt):.2f} +/- {np.sqrt(np.average((t[cov]-np.average(t[cov], weights=wt))**2, weights=wt)):.2f}"
                mc = f"{np.average(c[cov], weights=wc):.2f} +/- {np.sqrt(np.average((c[cov]-np.average(c[cov], weights=wc))**2, weights=wc)):.2f}"
        else:
            if cov in categorical_cols:
                mt = f"{t[cov].mean()*100:.1f}%"
                mc = f"{c[cov].mean()*100:.1f}%"
            else:
                mt = f"{t[cov].mean():.2f} +/- {t[cov].std():.2f}"
                mc = f"{c[cov].mean():.2f} +/- {c[cov].std():.2f}"
        fn = compute_smd_categorical if cov in categorical_cols else compute_smd
        smd = abs(fn(data, cov, treatment_col, weight_col))
        rows.append({'Variable': cov, 'Treated': mt, 'Control': mc, 'SMD': f"{smd:.3f}"})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A governed, source-agnostic healthcare semantic layer for both payer and provider. It has two parts over one canonical model: (1) a measure catalog — the correct, domain-grouped definitions of 64 healthcare measures that never change per customer; and (2) a build workflow — assess a customer's Databricks sources, map them to the canonical model, and generate Unity Catalog metric views consumable by Genie, AI/BI dashboards, Power BI, and agents. The only per-customer input is a source-mapping file; the catalog is fixed.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Look up the correct definition of a healthcare measure (ALOS, excess days, readmission rate, denial rate, net collection rate, slot utilization, MLR, PMPM) and whether it is additive.
  • Decide how a non-additive rate must be modeled in a metric view (ratio-of-measures, not average-of-averages).
  • Stand up a semantic layer for a provider system, a payer, or an integrated payer+provider customer.
  • Map Epic Clarity/Caboodle, X12 837/835/834 claims, OMOP CDM, or FHIR sources to governed metric views.
  • Generate care_delivery, claims, or payer_economics metric views for a specific customer schema.
  • Give a Genie space or an agent a governed measure layer instead of raw tables.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• MCP / tools: Databricks CLI authenticated to the target workspace (databricks current-user me -p <profile>); Python 3.9+ with PyYAML for the scripts.
  • Inputs: read access to the customer's source catalog/schema; a target catalog.schema and SQL warehouse_id for the generated layer.
  • Environment: a working directory for the engagement — all customer-specific artifacts (the mapping file, generated SQL) live there, never inside this skill.

docs.title: Quick Start

# 1. Copy the closest adapter as a starting mapping, edit sources for the customer:
#    references/adapters/{epic_clarity_caboodle,x12_837_835,omop_cdm,fhir}.yaml
# 2. Generate the layer from the mapping:
python3 scripts/generate_semantic_layer.py --mapping <customer>_mapping.yaml --out generated
# 3. Review generated/plan.md, then deploy generated/01_silver.sql and 03_metric_views.sql
#    to the target schema, and smoke-test:  SELECT MEASURE(<measure>) FROM <mv>

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Check for a mapping first. If the working directory already has a <customer>_mapping.yaml, use it and skip to Step 3. If there is no mapping file, profile the source to draft one — run scripts/profile_source.py --catalog <c> --schema <s> --warehouse-id <id> (or follow references/profiling.md to profile agent-driven when the script can't reach the workspace). Profiling writes <schema>_mapping.draft.yaml full of # REVIEW flags; confirm those (Steps 1–2), then generate.

docs.title: Step 1: Assess
docs.text:
Introspect the customer's source catalog/schema (information_schema / workspace files). Identify which canonical entities can be populated — that set decides which metric views are in scope. Pick the closest adapter(s) from references/adapters/.

SELECT table_name, column_name FROM <catalog>.information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = '<src>';

docs.title: Step 2: Map

Draft <customer>_mapping.yaml in the working dir — from the profiler's <schema>_mapping.draft.yaml (above) or from an adapter via extends:. Auto-map physical columns to canonical fields; flag low-confidence bindings with # REVIEW and confirm them with the user. See references/mapping_spec.md and references/profiling.md.

entities:
  encounter:
    source: <catalog>.<schema>.<table>
    fields: { encounter_id: ENC_CSN_ID, los_days: "datediff(disch, admit)" }
    enums:  { encounter_class: { source_column: ENC_TYPE_C, map: {"101": inpatient}, default: other } }

docs.title: Step 3: Generate

Run the generator. It infers scope (skips metric views whose entity is unmapped) and skips any measure whose canonical fields are missing — nothing broken is emitted. See references/mv_generation.md.

# -> generated/01_silver.sql, generated/03_metric_views.sql, generated/plan.md

docs.title: Step 4: Justify

docs.title: Step 5: Deploy & Expose
docs.text:
On explicit go-ahead, run 01_silver.sql then 03_metric_views.sql against the target schema, validate, and smoke-test each metric view. Then hand off to Genie and a starter Lakeview dashboard. See references/consumption.md.

SELECT MEASURE(avg_los_days), MEASURE(readmission_30day_count)
FROM <catalog>.<schema>.mv_care_delivery__encounter;

docs.text: Parameter Default Options Effect --mapping (required) path The per-customer source-mapping file --out generated path Output dir for the generated SQL + plan --skill / --plugin skill root path Where the catalog references live (rarely overridden) mapping scope.domains all mappable domain list Restrict which domains generate

docs.title: Expected Outputs
docs.text:
• generated/01_silver.sql — one conforming view per mapped entity (physical → canonical names, enum CASE, joins, filters).
  • generated/03_metric_views.sql — one mv_<domain>__<name> per in-scope metric view, atomics as aggregates and composites as MEASURE()/MEASURE().
  • generated/plan.md — the justify report (built vs skipped, with reasons).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• UNRESOLVED_COLUMN on deploy — the mapping references a physical column that does not exist. Fix the mapping's fields/enums, regenerate; the catalog and generator do not change.
  • DATATYPE_MISMATCH on a flag — a source flag is INT where a boolean is expected. Wrap it: CAST(<col> AS BOOLEAN) (robust to both int and boolean).
  • A metric view is missing — its entity was not mapped; check plan.md for the skip reason.
  • A measure is missing — a canonical field it needs is unmapped (e.g. no allowed_amount → net_collection_rate is skipped). Map the field or accept the reduced coverage.
  • A rate looks wrong on rollup — it must be a composite (MEASURE(a)/MEASURE(b)), never a stored or averaged rate. Run the validator.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Only what's mapped gets generated — unmapped entities silently drop their metric views.
  • Nothing customer-specific enters this skill — mappings, generated SQL, and secrets stay in the working directory.
  • Validate before deploy — python3 scripts/validate_catalog.py must report 0 errors; never deploy a measure that fails it.
  • Confirm before outward writes — deploying views/metric views and creating Genie spaces or dashboards are outward actions; show the plan and get explicit approval.
  • Never invent measures inline — if a customer needs one the catalog lacks, add it to the catalog (validate + render), then regenerate. Composites must be ratio-of-measures.
  • Run after any catalog edit: validate_catalog.py (correctness gate) then render_catalog.py (regenerate references/catalog.md).

docs.title: HLS Accelerators
docs.text:
Skill details

Version 1.0.0 · Author Rohan Parikh · License Databricks License

Browse on GitHub · Raw SKILL.md · Evaluation report

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Databricks publishes Health and Life Sciences solution accelerators under databricks-industry-solutions. Many requests ("index my DICOM files", "fold these proteins", "parse our HL7 ADT feed") are already solved by one of them. This skill routes the request to the right accelerator and ends with a precise next step: the exact library call, install command or admin action the user needs, plus the pitfalls that are not obvious from the README.

The skill is instructions only. It does not install or run accelerators itself. Per-accelerator facts live in references/accelerators/; the index is references/accelerators/index.md. Others can add accelerators by copying references/accelerator-template.md.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• A user wants to ingest, catalog or query DICOM images (CT, MR, X-ray) on Databricks, view them in a browser or auto-segment CT scans
  • A user wants protein structure prediction (AlphaFold2, ESMFold, Boltz) or protein design (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN) at scale
  • A user wants small-molecule generation, docking or ADMET/toxicity prediction
  • A user wants cell-type annotation against a reference atlas (SCimilarity), scGPT perturbation or a single-cell foundation model behind a UI
  • A user needs germline variant calling (NVIDIA Parabricks), GWAS, ClinVar annotation or NVIDIA BioNeMo fine-tuning
  • A user wants HL7v2 messages (ADT, ORU, ORM, SIU, VXU) from an EHR or interface engine parsed into Delta and queried with SQL
  • A user is about to hand-write a pipeline, parser or serving wrapper that an accelerator already provides

docs.title: Steer, do not rebuild
docs.text: The base model does not know these accelerators exist and will write pydicom loops or custom folding endpoints from scratch. Recommending the accelerator first saves days and avoids known failure modes.

docs.title: Precise next step
docs.text: Every answer ends with a short Next step section: one concrete action the user can take now (a command or snippet to run) and, if something is blocking them, the exact admin action and who does it. A link or "see the docs" is not a next step. The section repeats the literal command or code block to run first (for example the install line from the reference), even when the answer above is already a numbered procedure; "run the cells above", "write a plan" or "define the task" do not count.

docs.title: The repo is the source of truth
docs.text: Accelerators change weekly. Use the facts in references/accelerators/<name>.md for routing and pitfalls, then read the accelerator's own README and install docs for current steps. If the repo is cloned as a Git folder in the workspace, read the files there; otherwise give the user the repo URL and the exact file to open.

docs.title: Library path vs full install
docs.text: Some accelerators can be used as a Python library from a notebook (Pixels cataloging from a repo clone, check the serverless caveat in its reference; funke-hl7v2 parsing with %pip install from GitHub). Others are a full install of apps, jobs and GPU endpoints that needs workspace admin rights (Genesis Workbench, Pixels viewer and segmentation). Recommend the smallest path that answers the request.

docs.title: Accelerators are not supported products
docs.text: They are provided as-is without SLAs. Problems go to the repo's GitHub Issues, not Databricks support.

docs.title: Decision Framework
docs.text:
What is the user trying to do?
├── Medical imaging (DICOM)
│   ├── Index files, query metadata in SQL → Pixels, library path
│   ├── Browser viewer, DICOMweb endpoint, CT auto-segmentation → Pixels, full install
│   └── De-identify DICOM tags → Pixels DicomMetaAnonymizerExtractor
│       (structured tables instead → phi-deidentifier)
├── Life sciences models
│   ├── Proteins: fold, design, embed → Genesis Workbench large_molecule
│   ├── Small molecules: generate, dock, ADMET → Genesis Workbench small_molecule
│   ├── Single-cell foundation models (SCimilarity, scGPT, TEDDY) → Genesis Workbench single_cell
│   │   (notebook QC, clustering, markers → sc-rnaseq)
│   ├── Geneformer → Genesis Workbench bionemo; support is marked "coming soon",
│   │   so say so and offer the `open-weight-models` skill as the interim path
│   ├── Variant calling, GWAS, ClinVar → Genesis Workbench genomics
│   └── Model not shipped by Genesis Workbench → `open-weight-models` skill
└── Clinical messaging (HL7v2)
    ├── Parse message files into Delta, query fields with SQL → funke-hl7v2, library path
    ├── Streaming landing-to-parsed pipeline, ADT bed-utilization demo → funke-hl7v2, bundle
    └── FHIR, X12 claims or MLLP listener → not covered; say so
        (measures from parsed data → semantic-builder)
Task Accelerator Smallest path Reference Catalog DICOM files into a Delta table Pixels Catalog + DicomMetaExtractor references/accelerators/pixels.md OHIF viewer, DICOMweb, Vista3D segmentation Pixels Full install (admin) references/accelerators/pixels.md Protein structure prediction or design Genesis Workbench Full install: core + large_molecule (admin) references/accelerators/genesis-workbench.md Docking, molecule generation, ADMET Genesis Workbench Full install: core + small_molecule (admin) references/accelerators/genesis-workbench.md Single-cell foundation models Genesis Workbench Full install: core + single_cell (admin) references/accelerators/genesis-workbench.md Variant calling, GWAS, ClinVar Genesis Workbench Full install: core + genomics (admin) references/accelerators/genesis-workbench.md Parse HL7v2 message files into Delta funke-hl7v2 %pip install from GitHub + parse_hl7v2_msg UDF references/accelerators/funke-hl7v2.md Streaming HL7v2 pipeline or ADT demo funke-hl7v2 Asset Bundle deploy (no admin) references/accelerators/funke-hl7v2.md

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Route before writing code: Match the request to the Decision Framework, then read only that accelerator's reference.
  2. Check whether it is already deployed: Before proposing an install, ask the user or check the workspace for the signals listed in the reference (app, endpoint or table names). If it is deployed, point the user at it.
  3. Prefer the smallest path: Use the library path when it answers the request. Do not propose a full install to get DICOM metadata into a table.
  4. Name the blocker precisely: When an install needs admin rights or gated features, list exactly which ones and who enables them.
  5. Cite the repo and the file: Give the repo URL and the specific README or install doc section so the user can follow current steps.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. The accelerator does not cover the request: Recommending it anyway sends the user down a dead end.
    • How to avoid: Check the capability list in the reference; if nothing matches, say so and name the related skill.
  2. Install fails on a gated feature: Pixels needs Apps user token passthrough, Lakebase and Reverse ETL; Genesis Workbench needs workspace admin.
    • How to avoid: List prerequisites from the reference before giving install commands.
  3. Cloud-specific settings break the install: For example GPU_MEDIUM serving does not exist on Azure.
    • How to avoid: Ask which cloud the workspace runs on and apply the cloud notes in the reference.
  4. Code fails on serverless: Some accelerator notebooks and helpers assume classic compute (RDDs, /local_disk0, init scripts).
    • How to avoid: Ask which compute the user has and prefer the patterns the reference marks as serverless-safe.
  5. Resources deleted by hand break later deploys: Genesis Workbench tracks deployments with .deployed files and settings tables.
    • How to avoid: Remove modules only with ./destroy.sh <module> <cloud>.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Step 1: Classify the request
    • Map it to a row in the Decision Framework
    • Decision point: no match → say no covered accelerator fits and suggest the related skill
  2. Step 2: Read the reference
    • Open references/accelerators/<name>.md for capabilities, deploy signals, paths and pitfalls
  3. Step 3: Check the current state
    • Ask or check whether the accelerator is already deployed and which cloud the workspace uses
  4. Step 4: Answer and close with a Next step section
    • Library path: the install line and the minimal working snippet
    • Full install: prerequisites, commands in order, expected duration and the admin actions needed
    • Point to the repo's README or install doc for anything beyond the reference
    • Finish with Next step: the first command or snippet to run now, written out in a code block, then any admin action with the role that performs it

docs.title: Protocol Guidelines
docs.text:
1. One reference per accelerator: Copy references/accelerator-template.md to references/accelerators/<name>.md and add a row to references/accelerators/index.md.
  2. Stable facts only: References hold capabilities, deploy signals, prerequisites and the riskiest pitfalls. Step-by-step install text stays in the accelerator's repo.
  3. Record what was reviewed: Each reference lists the date and upstream commit it was checked against.
  4. Update this file only for routing: Add a Decision Framework branch and table row when a new accelerator is added.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:

Without the skill, Genie Code rebuilt a DICOM pipeline and a protein folding stack from scratch and gave wrong Pixels facts. The remaining tie (DICOM to Delta) reflects that Pixels' library did not install on serverless in testing; the skill now says so.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
1. Do not install or deploy accelerators on the user's behalf; give the commands and let the user or their admin run them.
  2. Do not claim an accelerator supports a model, format or cloud unless its reference or repo documents it.
  3. Treat accelerator outputs (segmentations, structure predictions, variant calls) as research results, not clinical or regulatory validation.
  4. Never suggest deleting accelerator resources in the workspace UI; use the accelerator's destroy or uninstall script.
  5. Avoid retrying more than 3 times; if an install step keeps failing, collect the task name and logs and point the user to the repo's GitHub Issues.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • Pixels - DICOM ingestion, OHIF viewer, DICOMweb, MONAI segmentation
  • Genesis Workbench - life sciences foundation models, workflows and MCP server
  • funke-hl7v2 - native HL7v2 parsing into Delta, streaming pipeline and ADT demo

docs.title: HLS Presentation Builder — Grounded, Shareable Decks
docs.text:
Skill details

Version 1.0.0 · Author Zachary Phillips · License Databricks License

Browse on GitHub · Raw SKILL.md

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Turns a finished HLS artifact into a self-contained HTML presentation a stakeholder can open in any browser and share — no server, no login, no PowerPoint. The deck renders onto a frozen design framework (fixed 1920×1080 canvas scaled to fit, keyboard/click navigation, one-slide-per-page "Save as PDF", Databricks branding), so the author only supplies a slide spec and the figures. What makes the output trustworthy is built in: every number on a data slide is grounded in the real artifact (pulled by ground.py and cited to its source table/column) and never typed by hand.

PHI handling is delegated, not re-implemented here: before building a deck from a patient-level source, de-identify it with the phi-deidentifier skill and build from its governed view. If phi-deidentifier is not available in the environment, the builder asks the user whether PHI may be included — see "De-identify before you present" below.

It runs on the execution model: Genie Code calls the vetted entrypoints and reports their output. It does not hand-write the ~400-line deck shell (that is frozen in scripts/deck_framework.py) and does not invent a figure (those come from ground.py).

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• "Turn this cohort into a deck I can send to the clinical team."
  • "Make a shareable presentation of the de-identified claims dataset."
  • "Present my model's evaluation metrics as slides for the review."
  • "Write up this analysis / measure catalog as an HTML one-pager to share."
  • "I need a readout deck for stakeholders — grounded in the real numbers, PHI-safe."
  • "Export the cohort summary as slides and let me Save-as-PDF."

For building the cohort itself use cohort-builder; to de-identify a table before it goes into a shareable deck use phi-deidentifier.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Compute: Python-enabled compute (serverless or a cluster) — NOT a SQL-only warehouse. The entrypoints are Python functions; ground.py uses the Databricks SDK to execute SQL against a warehouse on your behalf (auto-selected, or pass warehouse_id=). Auth is ambient in-workspace, or a CLI profile= locally. Rendering a deck needs no warehouse at all — only the grounding step queries data.
  • Inputs: a finished artifact to present — most often a Unity Catalog table/view (catalog.schema.table): a cohort, a de-identified dataset, a scored table, a measure catalog. Model metrics can come from an MLflow run / registered model you pass in as figures.
  • No external services are required to render; an optional Google-Fonts link loads DM Sans/DM Mono and degrades gracefully to system fonts offline.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "scripts")
import ground, build_deck

# De-identify FIRST if the source holds PHI: run the phi-deidentifier skill and point TABLE
# at its governed view. If phi-deidentifier isn't available, ask the user whether to include
# or exclude PHI before building (see "De-identify before you present").
TABLE = "catalog.schema.my_cohort_deid"

# 1) GROUND: pull real figures (each returns a `source` string to print on the slide).
head  = ground.cohort_summary(TABLE, profile="my-profile")          # N rows / N subjects
payer = ground.column_distribution(TABLE, "payer", profile="my-profile")  # bar data

# 2) ASSEMBLE a spec from those figures (never hand-type a number).
spec = {
  "title": "My Cohort", "footer_left": "Databricks · HLS",
  "slides": [
    {"type": "cover", "theme": "dark", "title": "My [[cohort]]",
     "subtitle": "Grounded, governed readout."},
    {"type": "metrics", "title": "Headline", "tiles": [
      {"value": f"{head['n_subjects']:,}", "label": "Patients", "caption": head["source"]}]},
    {"type": "bar_chart", "title": "By payer",
     "chart": {"heading": "Patients by payer", "unit": "patients", "bars": payer["bars"]},
     "notes": payer["source"]},
  ],
}

# 3) BUILD a single self-contained .html the user can open and share.
print(build_deck.build_deck(spec, "~/Downloads/my_cohort_deck.html"))

docs.title: Step 1 — Identify the artifact and the story
docs.text: Confirm what is being presented (cohort / dataset / model / analysis) and the audience (clinical, data, security, exec). Pick 5–8 slides. Keep one idea per slide.

docs.title: Step 2 — De-identify before you present (delegate to phi-deidentifier)
docs.text:
This skill does not detect, classify, or redact PHI — that is delegated. Before building a deck from any patient-/member-level source:

  1. Run the phi-deidentifier skill on the source table. It produces a de-identified, k-anonymous, governed Unity Catalog view (Safe Harbor) and a readout of what was removed. Point the grounding step (Step 3) at that view, not the raw table.

  2. If phi-deidentifier is NOT available in the environment — i.e. it is not installed in Genie or whatever LLM/agent is running this skill — do not guess, and do not quietly ship PHI. Stop and ask the user, e.g.:

    "The phi-deidentifier skill isn't available here, so I can't automatically redact PHI from <table> before putting it in a shareable deck. How would you like to proceed? (a) Include PHI as-is in the presentation (you confirm the source is already de-identified or that sharing identifiable data is acceptable), or (b) Exclude PHI — I'll present grounded aggregates only (counts, distributions, numeric summaries) and leave out patient-level rows."

    Build only after the user chooses. If they choose (b), stick to the ground.py aggregate helpers and do not place patient-level sample rows on any slide.

A non-PHI source (model metrics, a measure catalog, an already-de-identified view) needs no de-identification step — go straight to Step 3.

docs.title: Step 3 — Ground every figure (ground.py)
docs.text:
Pull the numbers from the data; never type them. Each helper returns a source string — put it in the tile caption or the slide notes so the deck is self-citing.

Helper Returns Use on slide cohort_summary(table) n_rows, n_subjects metrics tile numeric_summary(table, col) min/max/avg/median/count metrics tile column_distribution(table, col) bars (top-N value counts) bar_chart profile_table(table) row count, columns sanity / lineage

docs.title: Step 4 — Assemble the slide spec (vocabulary in references/deck_framework.md)
docs.text: Layout types: cover, statement, bullets, cards, metrics, bar_chart, two_column, architecture, closing. Per slide: theme (light/dark), kicker, title, subtitle, notes (speaker notes), footer_left. Inline markup in any text: [[x]] → accent highlight, **x** → bold. All content is HTML-escaped automatically.

docs.title: Step 5 — Build and verify (build_deck.build_deck)
docs.text:
build_deck.build_deck(spec, "~/Downloads/deck.html")
# -> {path, slides, bytes, titles}

Open the file in a browser. Navigate with ← / → / space / click (left half = back) / R to reset / End. Save as PDF: the browser print dialog emits one slide per page.

docs.title: Step 6 — Deliver
docs.text: Hand over the .html (self-contained — email it, drop it in Drive, host it anywhere). Note to the recipient that it is grounded in <table> — and, when the source held PHI, that it was de-identified upstream with phi-deidentifier (or that the user explicitly approved the PHI it contains).

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Where Meaning spec["slides"] build_deck the slides, each a layout dict (see references/deck_framework.md) spec["accent"] build_deck optional #hex brand accent override (default #ff3621) theme per slide "light" (default) or "dark" top ground.column_distribution keep the top-N categories by count (default 8) profile, warehouse_id ground.* CLI profile / warehouse for the grounding queries

docs.title: Expected Outputs
docs.text:
• A single self-contained .html file at out_path (open in any browser, email, host anywhere).
  • build_deck.build_deck(...) returns {path, slides, bytes, titles}.
  • ground.* helpers return figures plus a source string to print as the slide caption.
  • Navigation (←/→/space/click/R) and browser "Save as PDF" (one slide per page) work out of the box.

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• No hand-entered figures. Numbers on metrics/bar_chart slides must come from ground.py. If a figure isn't grounded, label it an assumption on a statement slide.
  • Sanity-check numeric figures before you print them. numeric_summary returns min and max alongside avg/median on purpose — eyeball them. Real tables (especially synthetic ones) carry impossible outliers (e.g. an HbA1c of 246,952%), which wreck a mean while leaving the median sane. Prefer the median, or filter the measure to a plausible range, and never put a mean on a slide without checking its min/max first. Grounding reports what's in the data — it does not launder it.
  • De-identify PHI upstream; never ship it silently. This skill does not redact PHI. For a patient-level source, run phi-deidentifier first and build from its governed view. If phi-deidentifier is unavailable, ask the user to include or exclude PHI (Step 2) and build only after they choose — do not decide on their behalf.
  • No editing the frozen framework. deck_framework.py is the locked shell; styling changes go in layouts.COMPONENT_CSS or the per-slide spec, never in the framework block.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The source table has PHI and phi-deidentifier isn't installed — don't build yet. Ask the user to include or exclude PHI (Step 2); if they exclude it, present grounded aggregates only and omit patient-level rows.
  • A distribution looks short / a category is missing — only the top top categories (by count, default 8) are returned; raise top to show more.
  • ValueError: unknown type ... / theme must be ... — the spec has a layout type or theme the renderer doesn't support; see the vocabulary in references/deck_framework.md.
  • Fonts look like the system default — the DM Sans/DM Mono webfont link needs network access; offline it falls back to system-ui by design (the deck is still self-contained).
  • Navigation / Save-as-PDF misbehaves — do not hand-edit deck_framework.py; regenerate the deck through build_deck so the frozen shell is emitted verbatim.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Path What it is scripts/build_deck.py Entrypoint: validate spec → render → write self-contained .html scripts/deck_framework.py Frozen deck shell (CSS, navigation runtime, print, protocol) scripts/layouts.py Pure slide renderers + the editable component CSS scripts/ground.py Grounded reads (counts/distributions/summaries), each cited to its source references/deck_framework.md Deck-spec contract + full layout vocabulary reference references/grounding_recipes.md SQL recipes for grounding figures + how PHI is delegated examples/build_example_deck.py Runnable worked example (a cohort readout deck) tests/ Offline unit tests (framework emission, renderer safety, grounding shape)

Design framework adapted from the OpenDesign deck runtime (open-design.ai). PHI de-identification is delegated to the phi-deidentifier skill (HIPAA Safe Harbor, 45 CFR §164.514(b)(2)).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Offline unit tests (tests/test_presentation_builder.py, no warehouse) assert the invariants: the frozen framework is emitted verbatim (navigation + print survive), the renderers are deterministic and HTML-escape all content (an unknown layout / empty deck / bad theme fails loud), and the grounding reader shapes figures the way the renderers expect. Run python3 -I -m pytest tests/ -q.

docs.title: LaTeX Report Builder
docs.text:
Skill details

Version 1.0.0 · Author Peter Hawkins · License Databricks

Browse on GitHub · Raw SKILL.md

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Generate structured scientific reports from notebook work: the agent writes a thorough Methods section (its primary deliverable), light Results with scientific highlights, and bullet-form Discussion — structured so the user can later expand them into a full paper. Compile to PDF entirely within Databricks using Tectonic.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• User asks to "write up", "summarize", "generate a report", or "make a PDF" from their notebook analysis
  • User wants to compile a .tex file to PDF inside Databricks
  • User asks for a methods/results summary of their work
  • User provides a .bib file and wants references included in the compiled report
  • User wants to iterate on a report: edit an existing .tex, recompile, and refine

docs.title: MANDATORY: Use the template
docs.text:
You MUST use one of the LaTeX templates from report-structure.md. This is non-negotiable:

  1. Read report-structure.md BEFORE generating any .tex content.
  2. Default to the REVTeX PRL preprint template unless the user explicitly asks for PRA or the internal report template. PRL produces a compact, professional layout; PRA is more spacious for longer reports.
  3. Start from the template's \documentclass and package list exactly as written.
  4. Fill in the <<PLACEHOLDER>> markers with real content from the notebook.
  5. Do NOT write LaTeX from scratch, do NOT invent your own document structure.
  6. If a section (e.g., Bibliography) is not needed, use \begin{thebibliography} with inline entries or omit it.
  7. REVTeX gotcha: Do NOT load hyperref (REVTeX loads it internally — duplicate loading causes parameter stack size overflow). Do NOT load float — use [htbp] instead of [H] for figure placement.

Both templates are tested and compile cleanly with Tectonic. Deviating from them risks compilation failures and wastes time.

docs.title: Step 1: Gather context
docs.text:
1. Read the source notebook with readAssetById. Identify:
    • What was done (methods: data sources, preprocessing, models, parameters)
    • Key results (metrics, statistics, findings, tables)
    • Figures (look for savefig, write_image, displayHTML, or any file writes to workspace/volume paths)
  2. Ask the user THREE things before proceeding (can be one message with all three):
    • "Where should I save the PDF?" — accept any workspace path or UC Volume path. Default suggestion: same directory as the source notebook, or a reports/ subfolder next to it.
    • "Do you have a .bib file for references, or should I skip the bibliography for now?" — bib is optional; most users will add it later during formal writing.
    • "To compile the report to PDF, I need to download the Tectonic LaTeX engine binary (~21 MB) from GitHub (github.com/tectonic-typesetting/tectonic), install it to /tmp, and run it to compile your .tex file. Do you permit me to download this binary from GitHub, install it, and use it?" — This explicit authorization is required. The phrasing must elicit the user's explicit consent to download, install, and execute a binary — all three verbs matter for the platform safety layer. Do NOT proceed to Step 2 until the user says yes.
    • The consent MUST be typed by the user in their own chat message. Do NOT collect this consent through askUserQuestions or any multiple-choice / button UI. A button click on an option the agent wrote (e.g., "Yes, download, install, and run Tectonic") is NOT treated as user-authored consent by the safety judge, and the download will be blocked (observed 2026-10-16). Instead, ask the question in plain chat text and ask the user to reply in their own words, for example: "I authorize you to download the Tectonic binary from GitHub, install it to /tmp, and run it to compile my report." The other two questions (output path, .bib) may still use a multiple-choice form. Why this gate exists: executeCode calls pass through an auto-approval judge that blocks downloads of third-party binaries unless the user has explicitly authorized them in the conversation. Without this consent on the record, even the 3-step split will be rejected. This is not optional ceremony — it is the mechanism that unlocks the download.

docs.title: Step 2: Ensure Tectonic is available
docs.text:
Prerequisites: - The user has explicitly authorized the Tectonic download in Step 1 in a message they typed themselves (not a button/form selection). If they haven't, go back and ask for a typed confirmation.

CRITICAL: Run these as THREE SEPARATE executeCode calls (chat compute), NOT one combined block, and NOT in notebook cells.

There are two safety layers that must both pass: 1. Auto-approval judge — reviews each executeCode call and blocks third-party binary downloads unless the user has explicitly authorized them in the conversation (Step 1). This is the most common blocker. 2. Single-cell filter — blocks code that downloads, extracts, and executes a binary in one cell. The 3-step split addresses this layer.

Both layers must pass. The 3-step split alone is NOT sufficient — the user's explicit consent from Step 1 is what satisfies the auto-approval judge. Always use executeCode (the agent's sandboxed chat compute) — notebook cells trigger a stricter safety review gate and may be rejected even with user consent.

The same three steps are shipped as tested, importable functions in scripts/ensure_tectonic.py (download(), extract(), verify()); the inline blocks below mirror it exactly.

Step 2a — Download (separate executeCode call): 

import os, urllib.request

TECTONIC_VERSION = "0.15.0"
TECTONIC_URL = (
    f"https://github.com/tectonic-typesetting/tectonic/releases/download/"
    f"tectonic%40{TECTONIC_VERSION}/"
    f"tectonic-{TECTONIC_VERSION}-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz"
)
TECTONIC_PATH = "/tmp/tectonic-bin/tectonic"
TECTONIC_ARCHIVE = "/tmp/tectonic.tar.gz"

if os.path.isfile(TECTONIC_PATH) and os.access(TECTONIC_PATH, os.X_OK):
    print(f"Tectonic already cached at {TECTONIC_PATH}")
else:
    print(f"Downloading Tectonic {TECTONIC_VERSION} (~21 MB)...")
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(TECTONIC_URL, TECTONIC_ARCHIVE)
    print(f"Downloaded: {os.path.getsize(TECTONIC_ARCHIVE):,} bytes")

Step 2b — Extract (separate executeCode call): 

import tarfile, os, stat

TECTONIC_DIR = "/tmp/tectonic-bin"
TECTONIC_PATH = f"{TECTONIC_DIR}/tectonic"
TECTONIC_ARCHIVE = "/tmp/tectonic.tar.gz"

if os.path.isfile(TECTONIC_PATH) and os.access(TECTONIC_PATH, os.X_OK):
    print(f"Tectonic already extracted at {TECTONIC_PATH}")
elif os.path.isfile(TECTONIC_ARCHIVE):
    os.makedirs(TECTONIC_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    with tarfile.open(TECTONIC_ARCHIVE, "r:gz") as tar:
        tar.extractall(TECTONIC_DIR)
    os.chmod(TECTONIC_PATH, os.stat(TECTONIC_PATH).st_mode | stat.S_IEXEC)
    os.remove(TECTONIC_ARCHIVE)
    print(f"Extracted: {os.path.getsize(TECTONIC_PATH):,} bytes")
else:
    print("ERROR: No archive found. Run Step 2a first.")

Step 2c — Verify (separate executeCode call): 

import subprocess, os

TECTONIC_PATH = "/tmp/tectonic-bin/tectonic"

if os.path.isfile(TECTONIC_PATH) and os.access(TECTONIC_PATH, os.X_OK):
    r = subprocess.run([TECTONIC_PATH, "--version"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(r.stdout.strip())
else:
    print("ERROR: Tectonic binary not found. Run Steps 2a and 2b first.")

After Step 2c, TECTONIC_PATH (/tmp/tectonic-bin/tectonic) is ready to use for compilation.

docs.title: Step 2d — If any step fails
docs.text:
Do not try anything else. No alternative compilers, no package managers, no workarounds — it is a waste of time.

Determine why it failed, then take the matching path:

  1. Auto-approval judge blocked the download (the error mentions safety, authorization, or blocked execution): The user's explicit consent from Step 1 was missing or not clear enough in the conversation. Tell the user exactly what happened and ask them to explicitly authorize the Tectonic download by typing it in their own chat message (a form/button answer is not sufficient). Once they do, retry Step 2a. Do not fall through to .tex-only delivery until the user has had the chance to authorize.
  2. Any other failure (network error, extraction error, binary won't run): Fall through immediately to Step 4, generate the .tex source and figures, and tell the user honestly what happened.

docs.title: Step 3: Prepare the build directory
docs.text:
import os, shutil, tempfile
build_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="latex-report-")

Copy into build_dir: - Any figures the user's notebook produced (from workspace files or Volume paths) - The user's .bib file if provided - The generated .tex file (see Step 4)

For figures: copy them into the build directory and use just the filename in \includegraphics. Supported formats: PDF (best for vector), PNG, JPG.

Strategy: Add a notebook cell that saves all figures as PNGs to the output directory (a UC Volume the user specified). Then use executeCode to read the figures from that Volume path, generate the .tex, compile, and deliver. This bridges the notebook state (which has the analysis objects) and the chat compute (which has Tectonic).

docs.title: Step 4: Generate the .tex file
docs.text:
See report-structure.md for the full LaTeX template and section-by-section guidance.

Key principles: - Results = scientific highlights only. A Results subsection should be a scientific finding ("CUX2-LAMP5 neurons are enriched in AD"), not a pipeline checkpoint ("Quality control retained 84.5% of cells"). If a subsection title could appear in the Methods of a published paper, it belongs in Methods, not Results. If no notable scientific findings emerged, the Results section can be a brief paragraph referencing the figures. - Methods = the agent's primary deliverable. Full journal-quality prose with every parameter, threshold, and rationale woven into sentences. No bullet lists of function calls. Include steps considered but rejected. See report-structure.md for the depth requirements. - Discussion = bullet-form. The agent flags patterns and interpretations; the user expands. - Include all figures. Every figure from the notebook gets a \begin{figure} with a descriptive caption summarizing what it shows. QC/diagnostic figures go in Methods, not Results. - Software versions: resolve programmatically. Before writing the .tex, run importlib.metadata.version(pkg) for every non-stdlib import in the notebook and embed exact versions. Never use \todo{verify} for versions when the notebook compute is available — query it. Use a multi-column table (Package/Version/Package/Version) to halve the height. - Breakable file paths. Use \fpath{} (defined in the template preamble) with \allowbreak after /, -, _, @ for any path longer than ~40 characters. Short identifiers stay as \texttt{}. Do NOT use \nolinkurl — it is unavailable in REVTeX. - Keep it compilable. Do not use packages beyond what the template provides. Tectonic auto-downloads packages, but exotic ones may fail. - No placeholder text. Every word in the report should be real content derived from the notebook. If you're unsure about something, flag it with % TODO: verify this in a LaTeX comment.

docs.title: Bibliography handling
docs.text:
• If user provides a .bib file: Copy it to the build directory. Add \bibliography{<filename-without-ext>} before \end{document}. Use \cite{key} in the text where appropriate.
  • If no .bib: Omit \bibliography and \bibliographystyle. The template handles this gracefully. Add a LaTeX comment % TODO: add bibliography at the bottom.
  • If user asks to generate references: You can create a .bib file with entries, but warn that citation details should be verified.

docs.title: Step 5: Compile
docs.text:
Skip this step if Tectonic is unavailable (Step 2d fallback). Jump to Step 6 and deliver the .tex + figures.

Compile with the TECTONIC_PATH verified in Step 2c:

import subprocess
TECTONIC_PATH = "/tmp/tectonic-bin/tectonic"
result = subprocess.run(
    [TECTONIC_PATH, "-X", "compile", "report.tex"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=build_dir, timeout=300,
)
if result.returncode == 0:
    print("PDF compiled successfully")
else:
    print(f"Compilation failed:\n{result.stderr[-2000:]}")

Tectonic handles everything in one invocation: auto-downloads packages, runs bibtex internally, re-runs TeX as needed to resolve references.

If compilation fails: 1. Check stderr for the specific error (usually a missing package or malformed LaTeX) 2. Fix the .tex content and retry — common issues: unescaped _, %, &, # in text; figure file not found in build dir 3. If it keeps failing after 2 retries, save the .tex source and tell the user what went wrong

docs.title: Step 6: Deliver the PDF
docs.text:
Copy the compiled PDF from the build directory to the user's chosen output path:

import shutil
shutil.copy2(os.path.join(build_dir, "report.pdf"), output_path)

Also offer to display it inline in the notebook/chat using:

import base64
from IPython.display import HTML, display
with open(pdf_path, "rb") as f:
    b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()
display(HTML(f'<iframe src="data:application/pdf;base64,{b64}" width="100%" height="800px"></iframe>'))

docs.title: Important constraints
docs.text:
• No hardcoded paths. Never assume a specific catalog, schema, volume, or workspace path. Always ask the user or derive from context. This skill is used across many different workspaces and organizations.
  • Tectonic downloads to /tmp only. The binary is session-scoped on the executeCode chat compute. Download is fast (~3-5s) and requires no shared infrastructure.
  • Figures must be copied to the build directory. LaTeX cannot reference arbitrary absolute paths reliably. Always copy figures alongside the .tex file.
  • Escape LaTeX special characters. When inserting notebook content into LaTeX, escape: _ → \_, % → \%, & → \&, # → \#, $ → \$, { → \{, } → \}. Exception: these characters inside \verb or verbatim environments, or when they're intentional LaTeX commands.
  • The report is a starting point. Remind the user that the output is structured notes for expansion, not a finished paper. Suggest they can iterate: edit the .tex, recompile, and refine.

docs.title: CRITICAL: Never improvise PDF generation
docs.text:
If LaTeX compilation is not available or fails: - DO save the .tex source file and all figures to the user's output path - DO tell the user honestly what happened and suggest alternatives (compile locally, try different compute) - DO NOT generate a PDF using matplotlib, reportlab, HTML-to-PDF, or any other non-LaTeX method - DO NOT silently substitute a different output format - DO NOT skip the .tex generation step — the source file IS the primary deliverable; the PDF is a convenience

The .tex file can always be compiled later by the user with any standard LaTeX distribution. A poorly-assembled non-LaTeX PDF cannot be edited, iterated, or submitted to a journal. The source is more valuable than a bad PDF.

docs.title: Graceful degradation priority
docs.text:
1. Best: .tex + figures + compiled PDF → user gets everything
  2. Good: .tex + figures, no PDF → user compiles locally or on different compute. Tell them exactly what files were saved and where.
  3. Unacceptable: Any improvised non-LaTeX PDF, or claiming compilation succeeded when it didn't

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Cause Solution Auto-approval judge blocks the Tectonic download User consent missing or collected via button/form instead of a typed message Ask the user to type the authorization in their own chat message, then retry Step 2a. Do not fall through to .tex-only delivery before giving them the chance Setup code rejected by the single-cell filter Download, extract, and execute combined in one cell Run Steps 2a, 2b, 2c as three separate executeCode calls parameter stack size overflow hyperref loaded manually in a REVTeX document Remove it — REVTeX loads hyperref internally Figure placement errors ([H]) float package loaded Use [htbp] placement instead; do not load float Compilation fails on text from the notebook Unescaped _, %, &, #, $, {, } Escape LaTeX special characters when inserting notebook content (see Important constraints) Network, extraction, or binary error in Step 2 Environment issue, not consent Fall through immediately to Step 4; deliver .tex + figures per the degradation ladder

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
1. Never proceed to Step 2 without the user's typed Tectonic authorization — a multiple-choice or button selection does not satisfy the auto-approval judge.
  2. Never improvise PDF generation — no matplotlib, reportlab, or HTML-to-PDF substitutes. The .tex source is the primary deliverable; the PDF is a convenience.
  3. Always start from the templates in references/report-structure.md; do not write LaTeX from scratch or invent document structure.
  4. No hardcoded paths — never assume a catalog, schema, volume, or workspace path; ask the user or derive from context.
  5. Tectonic installs to /tmp only — no package managers, no alternative compilers, no shared infrastructure.
  6. Max 2 compile-fix retries, then save the .tex source and tell the user exactly what went wrong.

docs.text:

  • REVTeX 4.2 — the default document class (PRL preprint and PRA templates)

docs.title: Scientific Figures Skill
docs.text:
Skill details

Version 1.0.0 · Author Peter Hawkins · License Databricks

Browse on GitHub · Raw SKILL.md

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This is the hub skill. It defines shared quality standards (size, fonts, color, layout, export) that apply to every figure, and routes to the right subskill reference file based on the visualization context. Subskill files live under references/ and are loaded on demand — do not load them all up front.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• User asks to create, style, or export a scientific figure, plot, or chart in a Databricks notebook
  • User needs a publication- or report-ready figure (journal PDF/PNG export, correct DPI and font sizes)
  • User asks for an interactive visualization (hover, zoom, dashboard embed) or is migrating a notebook plot into a Databricks App
  • User asks to render a protein structure, molecular surface, or binding site in 3-D (PDB/mmCIF)
  • User asks for a biopharma domain chart: Kaplan-Meier, forest plot, waterfall, swimmer, volcano, dose-response, CONSORT
  • Any life sciences analysis workflow that will produce figures as a side effect, even if the user only asked to "analyze"

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Route: match the request to subskill reference file(s) using the decision table below. Always load references/color.md alongside any rendering subskill.
  2. Set up: emit the notebook environment setup snippet (below) before the first figure.
  3. Plan the layout: apply the pre-render planning rules (legend placement, colorbar placement, panel count and width) before writing plotting code.
  4. Render: write the figure code in its own cell, separate from expensive compute.
  5. Review visually: fetch and inspect the rendered image against the design requirements checklist — mandatory for every figure (see "Mandatory visual review").
  6. Export: save both PDF and PNG with bbox_inches='tight'; for LaTeX-embedded figures, check effective font size after scaling.

docs.title: Decision: which subskill to load
docs.text:
Signal in the request Load subskill Any figure (always load, alongside the rendering subskill) color.md Static plot, publication PDF/PNG, journal submission, poster matplotlib-seaborn.md Interactive plot, hover tooltips, zoomable, HTML export, dashboard embed plotly-interactive.md Protein structure, PDB, mmCIF, molecular surface, binding site, 3-D render protein-structure-3d.md Protein-protein interface, chain contacts, interface residues, distance labels (only when asked; load with the protein subskill) protein-interface.md KM curve, forest plot, waterfall, swimmer, volcano, CONSORT, dose-response biopharma-domains.md

If the request spans multiple subskills (e.g. "interactive KM curve"), load both the domain subskill and the rendering subskill.

docs.title: Shared quality standards
docs.text: Apply these to EVERY figure regardless of library. These rules override any conflicting size, font or layout value in a subskill.

docs.title: Resolution and sizing
docs.text:
• Print / PDF: 300 DPI minimum, 600 DPI for line art.
  • Screen / notebook: 150 DPI is sufficient.
  • Databricks Apps: render at the container size; let the layout engine handle responsiveness. The width rule below does not apply to app components.

docs.title: Figure width (hard rule, applies to notebook and paper figures alike)
docs.text:
Layout Total figure width Derivation Single panel (one plot) ~3.15 in 90% of one journal column (3.5 in) 2+ panels side by side ~5.85 in 90% of letter text width (8.5 in page minus 1 in margins = 6.5 in)
  • The width covers everything: panels, legends, colorbars, panel letters and margins. Legends do not get extra width beyond the limit.
  • Never exceed 5.85 in for a static figure. If the content does not fit, reduce panels per row, move legends below, shorten labels, or split the figure. There is no "full-page 10 in" option (10 in is a page height).
  • Inherently wide single plots (KM with at-risk table, forest with estimate column, waterfall, swimmer, labelled volcano) start at 3.15 in and may widen up to 5.85 in only if the visual review shows they are cramped.
  • Single-panel figures with long labels: if a single-panel figure has category labels (axis ticks, legend entries) long enough that 3.15 in would leave less than 50% of the width for the actual plot area, use 5.85 in and mark it as figure* (full-width) in LaTeX. This is common with biological ontology terms, tissue names, and multi-word categories.
  • Exempt: interactive views (Plotly in notebooks/apps, 3-D viewers) are sized to their container; fonts still follow the 8 pt rule. Their static exports follow the width rule.
  • Posters, slides, or a specific journal's style guide: only when the user explicitly asks, using the size they specify. No default presets.
  • Height follows from the panel aspect rules below, not the other way round.
  • At 150 DPI these widths render at ~470 px and ~880 px in the notebook.

docs.title: Color
docs.text:
All color rules live in color.md: the company palette, the color-by-count order (black → red → navy → orange → teal → grey, max 6 hues), shade families for related groups, fixed semantic colors, cross-panel consistency and colormaps. Load it for every figure.

  • Background: white (#FFFFFF) for publications. For notebooks and apps, respect the Databricks theme if detectable; otherwise default to white.

docs.title: Typography
docs.text:
• Font family: Arial or Helvetica for journals (universal support). Inter or Source Sans Pro for digital/app contexts.
  • Font size (hard rule, at final printed size): 8 pt for all text — axis labels, tick labels, legends, colorbar labels, annotations, on-plot labels and panel letters.
    • Titles (figure and panel): at least 8 pt, bold. They may be larger, but never smaller.
    • 7.5 pt is the absolute floor. Nothing goes below it.
    • If text does not fit at 8 pt, change the layout (fewer panels per row, legend below, shorter labels, fewer on-plot labels). Do not shrink the font.
    • For figures embedded in a LaTeX report, "8 pt" means the effective size after LaTeX scales the figure to the column width. See "Font size compensation" under Export.
    • Posters: scale up proportionally from 8 pt.
  • Bold axis labels and tick labels by default — they read better at typical journal column widths. Drop bold only if a specific journal style guide prohibits it (e.g. some Cell Press templates). Title is always bold.
  • No suptitle for figures destined for LaTeX. The LaTeX \caption{} serves as the figure title. A matplotlib fig.suptitle() creates a duplicate title that either gets clipped (without bbox_inches='tight') or extends the PDF beyond the figsize (with tight), distorting the dimensions LaTeX expects. For notebook-only figures, suptitle is fine — keep it at y≤0.98 with adequate subplots_adjust(top=...) to prevent overlap with panel titles.
  • Long titles must wrap. If a title exceeds ~40 characters at the target figure width, insert a \n to wrap to two lines and add pad=12 to prevent collision with the plot area. This applies to ax.set_title(), colorbar labels, and legend titles.

docs.title: Pre-render layout planning
docs.text:
Before writing the plotting code, make these decisions based on the data:

Legends: Count the legend entries and estimate the longest label length. If entries × label length won't fit inside the axes at 8 pt, place the legend outside — below the figure with bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), loc='upper center', and ncol≥2. Never rely on a wrapper library's default legend placement for figures with >3 categories or labels >20 characters — auto-placed legends overflow the axes unpredictably.

Colorbars: If a colorbar is present, decide placement before rendering. Vertical colorbars on the right waste margin in narrow figures — use horizontal at top or bottom for figures ≤3.15 in wide. For multi-panel figures, prefer a single shared colorbar rather than one per panel.

Wrapper library overrides: Many plotting libraries (seaborn, plotly, domain-specific wrappers) auto-place legends and colorbars outside the axes. When using any wrapper library: 1. Suppress the auto-legend (the library's equivalent of "no legend") and build a manual fig.legend() with explicit bbox_to_anchor inside the figure bounds. 2. If the library adds an auto-colorbar, render first (make_figure() or equivalent), then find and hide the auto-placed colorbar axis, and add your own with controlled positioning via fig.add_axes(). 3. The specific suppression mechanism varies by library — check its docs. The principle is always the same: take control away from the default and place elements explicitly.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: • Use a fixed figsize in inches set by the width rule above. For multi-panel figures, size the panels first, then budget legends, gutters and margins in inches, and place axes explicitly (fig.add_axes in inch-derived fractions, or GridSpec with computed ratios). Never let leftover space after legends decide the panel shape — that is what produces stretched plots. tight_layout() / constrained_layout=True are acceptable for quick single-panel exploratory plots only.

docs.title: Panel aspect ratio (hard rule)
docs.text:
• Equal aspect (ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="datalim") or "box") is required whenever x and y share units or the geometry is meaningful: 2-D embeddings (e.g. PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), spatial / geographic / image coordinates, x-vs-y of the same quantity (predicted vs observed, replicate vs replicate, with a y = x line), correlation matrices and heatmaps (square cells), 2-D structure projections and maps.
  • Otherwise choose the box aspect for the data, not the leftover space: ~1:1 to 4:3 for scatter, violin, box and bar panels; wider (up to ~2:1) for time series, KM curves and dose-response. Avoid panels taller than wide unless the data is inherently vertical (forest plots, ranked lists, swimmer plots).
  • Plots of the same type in one figure share the same panel size.
  • Remove chartjunk: no background grid by default (add light grid only when it aids value reading, e.g. bar charts). Remove top and right spines for scatter and line plots.
  • Legend outside the plot area when >3 items; inside (upper-right or best) for ≤3 items.
  • Multi-panel: use subplot_mosaic or GridSpec for complex layouts. Label panels A, B, C in the upper-left corner, 8 pt bold.

docs.title: Default: always save both PDF and PNG
docs.text:
• Always save both formats when figures may be used in a report or shared. PDF for vector quality in LaTeX; PNG at 300 DPI for previews, slides, and web. The save_figure helper below defaults to formats=("pdf", "png").
  • PDF (.pdf): preferred for LaTeX \includegraphics. Vector text, axes, and spines stay crisp at any zoom. Preferred over SVG for LaTeX workflows.
  • PNG (.png): 300 DPI raster. Use for notebook display, slides, and web. Never .jpg for figures with text or line art.
  • Always save with bbox_inches='tight' for both PDF and PNG. This prevents clipping of titles, legends below axes, rotated tick labels, and colorbar labels that extend beyond the figsize — the most common source of broken figure PDFs. To keep saved dimensions predictable for LaTeX, design all content to fit within the figsize (see "Pre-render layout planning" below) — then bbox_inches='tight' acts as a safety net that captures any slight overhang without significantly changing the page size. If a figure's tight-cropped dimensions differ substantially from its figsize, that signals content is extending outside and the layout needs adjustment. Always print the final figure size in the cell output.
  • For Plotly: write_image (requires kaleido) for static export; write_html for interactive sharing.

docs.title: Font size compensation for report-embedded figures
docs.text:
When figures are embedded in a LaTeX report via \includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth], LaTeX scales each figure from its saved width to the column width. Because bbox_inches='tight' crops each figure differently (legends, colorbars, long labels all change the bounding box), the saved PDF widths vary — and so do the effective font sizes after scaling.

Default workflow (tight bbox with compensation):

  1. Start at 8 pt for all text (rcParams + every explicit fontsize= call). Use sns.set_context("paper", font_scale=0.8) before rcParams.update() so seaborn/scanpy internals also use small fonts.
  2. Save with bbox_inches='tight' (the default).
  3. Check the saved PDF width by reading the MediaBox: 
    import re
with open(pdf_path, "rb") as f:
    match = re.search(rb'/MediaBox\s*\[\s*[\d.]+\s+[\d.]+\s+([\d.]+)\s+[\d.]+\s*\]', f.read())
saved_width_in = float(match.group(1)) / 72
  4. Calculate the effective font size after LaTeX scaling: 
    effective_pt = source_pt × (target_width / saved_width)
    where target_width is 0.95 × \columnwidth (~6.18 in for REVTeX preprint).
  5. If effective size is off target, adjust the source font size: 
    adjusted_pt = round(target_pt × (saved_width / target_width), 1)
    Clamp: never let the effective size fall below 7.5 pt.
  6. Re-render with the adjusted font size and re-save. One iteration is usually sufficient — tight-bbox cropping is deterministic for a given layout.

Audit all font sources. Hardcoded fontsize=N calls, rcParams, and seaborn context all contribute. When changing font sizes, grep for every fontsize= in the notebook — not just the ones matching the current value. Different cells may have been set independently.

When to use manual layout instead:

If the user needs pixel-exact font consistency across all figures (e.g. strict journal style requirements), switch to non-tight saving: - Remove bbox_inches='tight' (set savefig.bbox to "standard") - Use explicit fig.subplots_adjust(left=..., right=..., ...) per figure - All figures save at exactly the figsize width → uniform scaling - This requires more per-figure iteration to avoid clipping, but guarantees identical effective font sizes across all figures

docs.title: Rasterization for large scatter plots (hybrid vector+raster PDFs)
docs.text:
Pure vector PDFs of scatter plots with >5,000 points become enormous and slow to render. Use matplotlib's rasterized=True on the scatter artist to produce hybrid PDFs: vector text, axes, spines, and legends with rasterized data points. This gives crisp text at any zoom while keeping file size manageable.

# Hybrid rasterization: vector chrome, raster data
ax.scatter(x, y, s=1, alpha=0.4, rasterized=True)  # data points rasterized
# Text, axes, legends remain vector — crisp at any zoom

When to use rasterized=True: - 2-D embeddings (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP — typically 5K–100K+ points) - Dense diagnostic scatter plots (e.g. residuals, QC metrics) - Any scatter with >5,000 points

When NOT to rasterize: - Bar charts, violin plots, box plots, line plots (already low element count) - Heatmaps (use imshow which is raster by default) - Dot plots (low element count)

Wrapper-library caveat: Some domain plotting libraries (e.g. scanpy, seaborn) pass rasterized= internally. If passing it again raises TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'rasterized', set rasterization on the axes instead: ax.set_rasterization_zorder(1) (rasterizes everything below zorder 1; data points default to zorder 0, text and axes are higher).

docs.title: Data ethics in figures
docs.text:
• Follow the workspace PHI rules: never plot individual patient identifiers. Aggregate to cohort, arm, or compound level for any figure that may be shared.
  • Axis labels must include units. Y-axis should start at zero for bar charts unless there is a strong analytical reason not to (document the reason in a comment).
  • Do not truncate axes to exaggerate effects without explicit annotation.

docs.title: Notebook workflow
docs.text: Always split expensive compute from plot rendering. Put data loading, metric computation, and threshold calculations in their own cell(s). Put the figure-drawing code in a separate downstream cell that only reads the computed variables. This lets you iterate on aesthetics (fonts, colors, sizing) without re-running the expensive pipeline — a round-trip that often takes minutes for large or compute-heavy datasets.

docs.title: Mandatory visual review (every figure, every render)
docs.text:
A figure is not done until the agent has looked at the rendered image and fixed what it sees. Code that runs without error is not evidence that the figure is correct.

Hard rule: every figure gets at least one visual review. No exceptions. After runAsset on any cell that produces a figure, the agent's next action MUST be getAssetExecutionResults (or equivalent) to fetch and inspect the rendered image. Do not add the next cell, do not proceed to the next analysis step, until the review is done. This applies to intermediate figures, final figures, and exploratory plots alike.

"Cell ran without errors" is not a visual review. A cell can succeed while producing overlapping text, clipped legends, or distorted aspect ratios — matplotlib does not raise exceptions for layout problems. The only way to catch these is to look at the pixels. If the image cannot be fetched (e.g. context limits), state that explicitly ("I could not fetch the rendered image for visual review") rather than silently skipping the check.

After fixing a figure, re-fetch and re-review. The fix itself may introduce new problems (e.g. moving a legend below may collide with x-axis labels). Every edit-run cycle must end with a fresh visual inspection.

docs.title: Review procedure
docs.text:
1. Render, then view. After running the plotting cell, fetch the rendered image (e.g. getAssetExecutionResults for the cell) and inspect it. If the run result only returns image metadata, fetch it explicitly.
  2. Confirm it is the new render. Print the figure size (and any changed parameter) in the cell output. If the image looks identical to the previous version after a code change, verify the live values in the session and re-fetch before drawing conclusions.
  3. Check against the design requirements (see below).
  4. Fix and repeat until the requirements pass (up to 3 rounds). Then report to the user what was checked and any residual issue that could not be fixed, instead of reporting the figure as finished.

Never describe a figure's appearance, or call it complete, without having viewed the current render.

docs.title: Design requirements checklist
docs.text:
These are the pass/fail criteria for every figure. Each item is either met or not met — there is no "close enough."

# Requirement Pass condition Common failure R1 Width Figure width matches the width rule (3.15 in single-panel, ≤5.85 in multi-panel). Saved file matches designed size. tight_layout or bbox_inches='tight' silently changed the width. R2 Aspect ratio Equal aspect where required (embeddings, spatial, correlation). Otherwise panels are ~1:1 to 4:3. Nothing looks stretched or squashed. set_aspect missing on embedding plots; leftover space dictating panel shape. R3 No text overlap No overlapping or clipped text, labels, legends, or panel letters. All text fully visible. Long legend entries or axis labels running into adjacent panels or data. R4 No dead space No large empty gutters, oversized margins, or wasted whitespace. right=0.72 leaving 28% empty when legends are short. R5 Font sizes 8 pt for all text (7.5 pt floor). Titles ≥8 pt bold. Any hardcoded fontsize= below 7.5 is a failure. For report-embedded figures, check effective size after LaTeX scaling. Legend or tick labels dropped below 7.5 pt "to fit". R6 Color Palette from color.md only. Count order respected. Max 6 hues. Same category = same color across panels. Neighbors distinguishable. Default matplotlib colors used instead of company palette. R7 Legends Complete (every visual encoding explained). Not redundant with on-plot labels. Readable names (no raw column names or opaque IDs). Legend shows internal identifiers instead of human-readable names. R8 Axis labels Every axis has a label. Units included where applicable. Embedding axes unlabeled; count axis missing units.

docs.title: Two-tier review standard
docs.text:
Standard review (interactive analysis): Every figure gets at least one pass through the checklist. Fix any R3 (text overlap) or R5 (font size) failures immediately — these are never acceptable. For R1, R2, R4, R6–R8, fix if possible within 1–2 edits; note residual issues to the user if not.

Report-generation review (PDF/LaTeX export): Figures destined for a report or publication must pass all 8 requirements before export. The agent must iterate (up to 3 rounds) until all pass, or explicitly flag which requirements could not be met and why. A figure that fails any requirement must not be silently included in a report.

docs.title: Acknowledging the review
docs.text: After reviewing, state what you checked and any issues found — even if everything passed. Example: "Reviewed: 5.85×4.0 in, equal aspect on embeddings, no text overlap, 10pt legend (single-panel floor), palette correct." If you cannot state what you checked, you did not review.

docs.title: Notebook environment setup snippet
docs.text:
When generating the first figure in a notebook session, emit this setup cell before the figure code:

import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# -- Scientific figure defaults ------------------------------------------------
_FIGURE_STYLE = {
    # Canvas
    "figure.figsize": (5.85, 4.0),   # multi-panel max width; single panel 3.15 in
    "figure.dpi": 150,
    "savefig.dpi": 300,
    "savefig.bbox": "tight",      # safety net; content should fit in figsize; see Export
    "savefig.pad_inches": 0.05,
    "savefig.transparent": False,
    # Font
    "font.family": "sans-serif",
    "font.sans-serif": ["Arial", "Helvetica", "DejaVu Sans"],
    # 8 pt everywhere; titles >= 8 pt; absolute floor 7.5 pt
    "font.size": 8,
    "axes.titlesize": 8,
    "figure.titlesize": 8,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold",
    "figure.titleweight": "bold",
    "axes.labelsize": 8,
    "xtick.labelsize": 8,
    "ytick.labelsize": 8,
    "legend.fontsize": 8,
    "legend.title_fontsize": 8,
    # Axes
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": False,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.8,
    # Lines and markers
    "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
    "lines.markersize": 5,
    # Legend
    "legend.frameon": False,
    # Color
    "axes.prop_cycle": mpl.cycler(
        color=["#000000", "#D62728", "#3A6EA5", "#F28C28", "#1BA7A6", "#8C8C8C"]
    ),  # color.md Rule 1 order: black, red, navy, orange, teal, grey
    "image.cmap": "viridis",
}
# seaborn context/style OVERWRITE font sizes: call them first, then our rcParams.
# "paper" context with font_scale=0.8 keeps seaborn/scanpy internals near 8pt.
sns.set_context("paper", font_scale=0.8)
sns.set_style("ticks")
mpl.rcParams.update(_FIGURE_STYLE)

# NOTE: Some domain libraries (e.g. scanpy) override rcParams on import.
# Re-enforce after their imports: mpl.rcParams.update(_FIGURE_STYLE)

print("Scientific figure defaults applied.")

docs.title: Saving figures from notebooks
docs.text:
When the user wants to save a figure to a UC Volume or workspace path:

import os

def save_figure(fig, name, path, formats=("pdf", "png"), dpi=300):
    """Save a matplotlib figure in one or more formats.

    `path` is a UC Volume or workspace directory the user has chosen — ask
    for it; do not assume a default. Always uses bbox_inches='tight' to
    prevent clipping. Design all content to fit within the figsize so tight
    acts as a safety net, not a layout tool.
    """
    os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True)
    for fmt in formats:
        out = os.path.join(path, f"{name}.{fmt}")
        fig.savefig(out, format=fmt, dpi=dpi, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0.05)
        print(f"Saved: {out}")
    w, h = fig.get_size_inches()
    print(f"Figure size: {w:.2f} x {h:.2f} in")

docs.title: App context detection
docs.text:
When the user's figure is destined for a Databricks App rather than a notebook or PDF, switch guidance:

  1. Simple interactive chart (no complex UI): stay in Plotly; use references/plotly-interactive.md.
  2. Rich app with controls, forms, multi-view: recommend migrating to a React + Plotly.js or React + Deck.gl stack. See the migration section in references/plotly-interactive.md.
  3. 3-D molecular viewer in an app: use Molstar (not py3Dmol). See references/protein-structure-3d.md.

docs.title: Quick reference: library selection
docs.text: Need Library Notes Static publication figure matplotlib + seaborn Best control, universal journal acceptance Quick EDA in notebook seaborn / pandas .plot() Fastest iteration Interactive exploration Plotly Hover, zoom, filter; good notebook support Interactive in Databricks App Plotly (simple) or React + Plotly.js (complex) See app migration guide Protein / small molecule 3-D Molstar (default: core CDN in notebooks, React in apps); py3Dmol if the user wants simple Python or asks for it Try Molstar first; NGL only as a last resort after telling the user. See protein subskill Geospatial / map overlays Plotly Mapbox or Folium Not covered in depth here Animated figures matplotlib FuncAnimation or Plotly frames Use sparingly; prefer faceting

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Cause Solution Saved figure width differs from figsize bbox_inches='tight' cropped overhanging content Content is extending outside the figsize — fix layout; treat tight as a safety net, not a layout tool Overlapping or clipped text/legends Auto-placed legend from a wrapper library, or labels too long for the width Suppress the auto-legend; place a manual fig.legend() below the axes; wrap long titles with \n TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'rasterized' Domain library (scanpy, seaborn) passes rasterized= internally Use ax.set_rasterization_zorder(1) instead of passing rasterized=True Fonts too small in a LaTeX-embedded figure Tight-cropped PDF widths vary, so LaTeX scaling changes effective font size Read the MediaBox width, compute effective pt, adjust source font size and re-render (see Export) rcParams reset after import Some libraries (e.g. scanpy) override rcParams on import Re-apply mpl.rcParams.update(_FIGURE_STYLE) after their imports Plotly static export fails write_image requires kaleido Install kaleido, or use write_html for interactive sharing instead

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
1. Every figure gets a visual review. Never call a figure done without fetching and inspecting the rendered image; re-review after every fix (max 3 rounds, then report residual issues).
  2. Never shrink text below 7.5 pt to make content fit — change the layout instead.
  3. Never exceed the width rule (3.15 in single-panel, 5.85 in multi-panel) for static figures.
  4. No individual patient identifiers in figures. Aggregate to cohort, arm, or compound level for anything that may be shared.
  5. Do not truncate axes to exaggerate effects without explicit annotation; bar charts start at zero unless justified in a comment.
  6. Confirm with the user before heavy rendering workloads (e.g. >100k-point 3-D views or batch figure generation).
